quiz.p: Which three things does every fire need?
quiz.why: Every fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat at once. Smoke, light and ash are what a fire gives out, not what it needs.

quiz.p: A box of matches sits on a shelf. It has fuel and air all round it. Why doesn't it catch fire?
quiz.why: The matches have fuel and air, but they need heat to start. Striking a match on the box gives that heat. Picking 'no oxygen' is a fair try, but the air all round the box has oxygen.

quiz.p: In The Jumping Flame, a match held in the white smoke of a blown-out candle relit the wick. What was burning in the smoke?
quiz.why: Just after the candle went out, wax gas kept rising from the hot wick. The match lit that gas, and the flame ran down it to the wick. Picking 'the air' is a good thought, because oxygen from the air was needed too. But the air alone does not burn.

quiz.p: A grown-up held a lit match to a lump of wax with no wick. What happened?
opts: It melted a little but did not keep burning
quiz.why: The heat spread into the big lump and only melted it. Not enough wax turned into gas in one place to keep a flame going. A wick fixes that by lifting a little melted wax into the hottest part of the flame.

quiz.p: Oil in a kadai catches fire. What should a grown-up do?
opts: Pour a mug of water on it
Turn off the stove and cover the kadai with a lid
Carry the kadai to the sink
quiz.why: Turning off the stove stops the heat, and the lid keeps the air away. Water sinks under the hot oil, turns to steam at once and throws the burning oil out. Carrying a burning kadai can spill burning oil.

quiz.p: Firefighters spray water on a burning wooden house. Which side of the fire triangle does the water mostly take away?
quiz.why: Water cools the burning wood below the heat it needs to keep burning. Steam from the water also pushes some air away, so oxygen is a fair second answer.

quiz.p: Farhan's kurta catches fire from a lamp. What should he do?
opts: Stop, drop to the ground, cover his face and roll
Wave his arms to blow the fire out
quiz.why: Rolling keeps the air from the flames, so they go out. Running and waving bring more oxygen, so the fire burns harder.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, burns her finger on a hot vessel. What is the best first aid?
quiz.why: Cool running water takes the heat out of the skin. Toothpaste and ice feel cool for a moment but do not cool the burn deep down, and can harm the skin.

quiz.p: Why does cooking gas have a strong smell?
opts: Cooking gas always smells like that naturally
A smell is added so that people notice a leak
The smell is the gas burning
quiz.why: The gas itself has almost no smell. A strong-smelling chemical is added, so that a leak can be noticed before a spark lights it.

quiz.p: How did early people make fire, before matches?
opts: By spinning a stick fast against wood, or striking stones to make sparks
By leaving wood in the sun
quiz.why: Rubbing makes heat by friction. A spinning stick can make a glowing ember. Some stones give sparks when struck. Sunlight alone does not light wood, unless it is focused with a lens.

quiz.p: What is the oldest clear sign that people used fire?
opts: Burnt bones and plant ash in a cave in South Africa, about one million years old
Drawings of fire on the Moon
quiz.why: In Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, scientists found burnt bones and ash from plants about one million years old. Scientists still argue about when fire became part of everyday life.

quiz.p: Humphry Davy put a lamp's flame inside a cylinder of fine iron mesh. Why could the flame not light the gas outside?
opts: The mesh kept out all the gas
The metal took heat away, so the gas outside was too cool to burn
The mesh made the flame smaller
quiz.why: Gas could pass through the mesh and burn inside it. But the metal took heat from the flame, so the gas outside stayed too cool to catch fire. You saw this with a tea strainer over a candle.

items.p: The three sides of the fire triangle are fuel, oxygen and ____.
items.why: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat at the same time.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a fuel, or not a fuel?
items.a: see items
items.why: Fuels can burn and give out heat. Water, sand and steel do not burn in a home fire. A strong sorter thinks about whether the thing can burn, not whether it is hot.

items.p: In The Jumping Flame, a match held in the white smoke relit the candle without touching the wick. Explain what was in the smoke.
items.a: The smoke had wax gas in it, still rising from the hot wick. The match lit the gas, and the flame ran down the gas to the wick.
items.why: A strong answer says the smoke carried wax gas, and that the flame followed the gas down to the wick.

items.p: Ranjani blows out a birthday candle. What does her breath do to the flame?
items.why: Her breath pushes the wax gas away from the wick and cools the wick, so the flame has no fuel near enough to keep going. Picking 'adds water' is a guess about breath being damp, but that is not what puts it out.
opts: Pushes the wax gas away and cools the wick

items.p: A lump of wax lights as easily as a candle wick.
items.why: False. In The Jumping Flame, a match held to a lump of wax only melted it. The wick lifts a little melted wax into the flame, where it turns into gas and burns.

items.p: Draw a candle burning. Add arrows to show the melted wax climbing the wick and turning into gas at the flame.
items.a: A candle with a pool of melted wax at the top, an arrow going up the wick, and a label 'wax gas' just under the flame.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the wax melting first, then climbing the wick, then turning to gas near the flame.
items.art: A blank box with a candle outline drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Match each way of putting out a fire to what it takes away.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each way of putting out a fire takes away one side of the fire triangle.
pairs: a lid on a burning kadai

items.p: Meenakshi's grandmother says, "Tie back your davani before you light the lamps." Give the reason behind this rule.
items.a: A loose davani is cloth, which is a fuel. If it swings into the flame, the flame's heat can light it, and the air around it lets it burn.
items.why: A strong answer names the fire triangle: the cloth is fuel, the lamp gives heat and the air gives oxygen.

items.p: Which of these should a child never do?
items.why: Matches and lighters stay with grown-ups, because a child may not be able to control the flame or put it out. The others are good habits.
opts: Tell a grown-up if you smell gas
Keep a lamp on a steel plate

items.p: Put these in order, for a small burn on your hand.
a: Move away from the hot thing
Hold the burn under cool running water
Cover it loosely with a clean cloth
items.why: First get away from the heat. Then cool the burn for a full 20 minutes. Only after that, cover it loosely.
items: Cover it loosely with a clean cloth
Hold the burn under cool running water
Move away from the hot thing

items.p: Smoke rises, so the cleanest air in a smoky room is near the floor.
items.why: True. Hot smoke rises to the ceiling first. That is why you crawl low to get out.

items.p: If your clothes catch fire: stop, ____, and roll.
items.why: Stop, drop and roll. Dropping and rolling press the flames against the ground and keep the air away.

items.p: In India, which number do you call for the fire service?
items.why: 101 is the fire service. 112 also works for any emergency, including fire.

items.p: Arjun says, "Smoke is just air that has been burnt, so it can't hurt you." Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. Smoke carries tiny bits of soot and poisonous gases. In house fires, more people die from breathing smoke than from the flames.
items.why: A strong answer says what smoke contains, and why that matters in a fire.

items.p: Farhan's family is deciding whether he, aged 9, may light the pooja lamp.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a reason from the unit, such as the fire triangle, the steel plate, or the matches staying with grown-ups. It then gives one fair point from another side.
items.why: There is a real trade-off. Children learn care by doing, but matches and loose clothes need a grown-up's control.

views.says: He can light it with a long match, with me beside him. He learns to respect fire by using it carefully.
Not until he is older. Matches are for grown-ups, and one slip can set his kurta on fire.
I can put the lamp on the steel plate and fill the oil. A grown-up can do the match.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.

items.p: Draw the fire triangle. Write fuel, oxygen and heat on its sides. Then draw one way to take away each side.
items.a: A triangle labelled fuel, oxygen and heat, with, for example, a gas regulator turned off by fuel, a lid by oxygen, and water by heat.
items.why: A strong drawing matches each way of putting out a fire to the right side.

items.p: In Dry Wick or Oiled Wick?, the dry wick burned for under a minute, but the wick in oil burned for 10 minutes. What was the main fuel in the oiled diya?
items.why: The oil climbed the wick and burned as a gas at its tip. The soaked cotton hardly burned. Picking 'the cotton' is natural, because the flame sits on it, but the dry wick showed how fast cotton alone burns away.

items.p: Why does a diya's wick hardly get shorter while there is oil, but burn away quickly when the oil runs out?
items.a: While oil keeps climbing, the oil turns to gas and burns at the tip, and the soaked cotton stays cool enough not to burn. When the oil runs out, the cotton is the only fuel left, so it burns away.
items.why: A strong answer says the oil is the fuel and protects the cotton by keeping it soaked.

items.p: Cooking gas lights more easily than candle wax because it is already a gas.
items.why: True. A flame burns gas. Wax must first melt and turn into gas, but cooking gas is ready to burn the moment a spark reaches it.

items.p: A big log will not light from one match, but a handful of thin dry twigs will. Why?
items.why: Thin twigs heat up quickly all the way through, so they give off gas fast. In a big log, the heat spreads into the wood and only warms it. Picking 'logs have no fuel' is not right, because a log burns well once a twig fire is under it.
opts: Thin twigs heat up quickly and give off burning gas
Logs have no fuel in them
Twigs have more oxygen inside them

items.p: The yellow glow of a candle flame comes from tiny hot bits of ____.
items.why: Tiny bits of soot glow yellow in the heat. A gas stove flame has very little soot, so it is blue.

items.p: Two cousins are arguing about blowing on fires.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are partly right. Blowing on a candle pushes the small amount of wax gas away and cools the wick. Blowing on embers brings more oxygen than it takes heat away, so they burn harder.
items.why: This is a real puzzle with two true sides. What blowing does depends on how big the fire is and how much fuel and heat it has.

views.says: Blowing puts out fires. I blow out my birthday candles every year.
Blowing makes fires bigger. Paati blows through a pipe to get the chulha going.

items.ask: Who is right? Use the fire triangle to explain. Then say what the other cousin has right.

items.p: Sort these into what a candle flame takes in and what it gives out.
items.a: see items
items.why: A flame takes in wax gas and oxygen. It gives out heat, light, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and sometimes soot.

items.p: Why is it dangerous to keep petrol or kerosene near a flame, even when they are cold?
items.why: Petrol and kerosene give off flammable gas even at room temperature. That gas can spread and reach a flame. Picking 'they are hot inside' is not right: the danger is the gas they give off.
opts: They give off flammable gas even when cold

items.p: In the Tea Strainer Test, the fine mesh stopped the flame. Draw what you saw from the side: the candle, the flame and the mesh. Show where the smoke went.
items.a: A candle, a flame flattened under the mesh, and smoke rising above the mesh.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the flame below the mesh only, with smoke passing through.

items.p: In the Tea Strainer Test, the fine mesh stopped the flame but let smoke through. What did the metal do to the flame?
items.a: The metal wires took heat away from the burning gas. The gas that got through the mesh was too cool to burn, so the flame stayed below.
items.why: A strong answer says the metal carried heat away, and that the gas above was too cool to burn.

items.p: Match each fire to the best way to put it out.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The right way depends on the fuel. Water is good for wood, but never for oil.
pairs: turn off the stove and cover with a lid
a burning heap of dry leaves
a small fire on a cloth
smother it with a wet towel or roll on it

items.p: Burning is a change that can easily be undone, like melting.
items.why: False. Burning makes new substances, such as carbon dioxide and water. You cannot turn ash and smoke back into wood. Melting wax can be undone by cooling it.

items.p: Nila holds a cold steel spoon in a yellow candle flame for a moment. It comes out black. What is the black stuff?
items.why: It is soot: tiny bits of carbon from wax gas that did not burn fully. A blue gas stove flame leaves much less.

items.p: Early people often carried glowing embers with them from camp to camp, instead of making a new fire each time. Why might they have done that?
items.a: Making fire by spinning a stick or striking stones was slow and hard, and might fail when wood was damp. Carrying an ember was easier. Covered with ash, an ember can keep burning slowly for hours.
items.why: A strong answer says making fire was hard, and that an ember kept slowly burning, with little air, until it was needed.

items.p: Put these steps of a burning candle in order.
a: Heat turns the wax into gas
The gas burns and makes more heat
items.why: This loop keeps the candle going: the heat from the burning gas melts more wax.
items: The gas burns and makes more heat
Heat turns the wax into gas

items.p: Divya smells gas when she comes home. What should she NOT do?
items.why: A light switch can make a tiny spark that lights the gas. Opening windows and telling a grown-up are both right.

items.p: In 1816, people argued about Humphry Davy's safety lamp for coal miners.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence: the mesh does stop a flame, as the tea strainer showed, but a draught or a broken wire could let it out, and the lamp led owners to send men into more dangerous places. It then gives the other side its due.
items.why: Both were partly right. The lamp worked as a light in firedamp, but the 1835 committee found accidents had gone up.

views.says: The Davy lamp makes my mine safe. Now my miners can dig in the gassy parts too.
The lamp's light is dim, and if a wire breaks the flame gets out. The gas is still there.
The mesh cools the flame so it cannot get out. Used carefully, the lamp is safe.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give evidence from this unit. Then say what one other person had right.

items.p: In The Jumping Flame, the flame jumped down from 2 cm every time but from 8 cm only sometimes. Explain why height made a difference.
items.a: Close to the wick, the wax gas is thick enough to burn. Higher up, it has spread out and mixed with more air, and some has cooled into droplets, so there is too little gas in one place to carry the flame down.
items.why: A strong answer links height to how much wax gas there is in one place.

items.p: Nila closed the lid on the glass jar round her diya, and the flame slowly went out. The diya still had oil. Which side of the triangle was missing?
items.why: With the lid on, no fresh air could get in, so the flame ran out of oxygen. It still had oil, and the wick was still hot.

items.p: A flame needs a match only to start. After that, it makes its own heat.
items.why: True. The flame's heat melts the wax and turns it into gas. That gas burns and makes more heat. The loop goes on until the fuel or the air runs out.

items.p: A fire has been put out with water, but the wood is still hot. Why might a fire fighter keep spraying it?
items.a: The wood still has fuel and air around it. If it stays hot enough, it can start burning again. Cooling it fully takes away the heat side of the triangle for good.
items.why: A strong answer says all three sides could come back together if the wood stays hot.

items.p: Coal miners in the 1700s used a spinning steel wheel that threw sparks for light. They thought it was safer than a candle. Why was it still dangerous?
items.why: A spark is a tiny hot bit of metal. It is hot enough to light firedamp gas. An explosion at Wallsend Colliery in 1785 showed this.
opts: Sparks are hot enough to light firedamp
Sparks use up all the oxygen
The wheel was too heavy to carry

items.p: Put these events in time order, oldest first.
a: People in Wonderwerk Cave leave burnt bones and ash
Hearths are common in caves in many places
Safety matches are made in Sweden
items.why: About one million years ago, about 400,000 years ago, 1815, and the 1840s to 1850s.
items: Hearths are common in caves in many places
Safety matches are made in Sweden
People in Wonderwerk Cave leave burnt bones and ash

items.p: Many people think a candle burns its wick, like a slow fuse. Use two results from this unit to show what really burns.
items.a: In The Jumping Flame, the flame lit the smoke and ran down to the wick, so wax gas burns. In Dry Wick or Oiled Wick?, the wick in oil hardly got shorter in 10 minutes, but the dry wick burned away in under a minute. So the fuel is the wax or oil, burning as a gas.
items.why: A strong answer uses two pieces of evidence and says what each one shows.

items.p: Why does a gas stove flame look blue, while a candle flame looks yellow?
items.why: In a gas stove, air is mixed with the gas before it burns, so it burns fully and makes very little soot. In a candle, soot forms inside the flame and glows yellow.
opts: Air is mixed into the gas first, so it burns fully with little soot

items.p: Richard Wrangham thinks learning to cook changed human bodies. Which fact supports his idea?
items.why: Cooked food gives the body more energy and needs less chewing, which fits with smaller teeth and guts and bigger brains. The other two are true facts, but they do not support his idea.
opts: Cooked food gives more energy and needs less chewing
Fire was on Earth before people

items.p: Design a lamp for a coal mine, using what you learned about metal mesh. Label the flame, the mesh, and where air comes in.
items.a: A flame inside a cylinder of fine metal mesh, with air coming in through the mesh and a solid top or shield.
items.why: A strong design keeps the flame completely inside fine metal mesh, and lets air in through it.

items.p: Draw a timeline from early people keeping fire to you lighting a gas stove. Put at least four steps on it.
items.a: For example: keeping fires from wildfires, carrying embers, making fire with a fire drill, oil lamps, matches, gas stoves.
items.why: A strong timeline puts the steps in a sensible order and shows how making fire got easier.

items.p: A forest fire is coming towards a village. Fire fighters cut down and clear a wide strip of dry bushes in front of it. Which side of the fire triangle does this take away?
items.why: With no dry plants left in the strip, the fire runs out of fuel when it reaches it. This kind of strip is called a firebreak.

items.p: A strip of land cleared of plants to stop a forest fire is called a fire____.
items.why: A firebreak takes away the fuel, so the fire cannot cross it.

items.p: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, said the world is like an ever-living fire. A candle flame looks the same all hour, but its gas is new every moment. Do you think it is the same flame all hour? Give your reason.
items.a: Any answer with a reason is good. For example: yes, because it keeps the same shape and place. Or: no, because the gas in it now is different from the gas a minute ago.
items.why: This is an open question. A strong answer uses what a flame is made of to explain its view.

applications: Cooking on a gas stove, a chulha or a wood fire.
Lamps and candles for light in a power cut, and diyas at festivals.
Firefighting: water, foam, sand and fire blankets each take away one side of the fire triangle.
Firebreaks cleared in forests to stop wildfires spreading.
Flame arresters, a mesh like Davy's, inside some fuel cans and gas pipes.
Smoke alarms that sound when they sense smoke.
Matches and lighters, which give the first heat.
Engines in cars, buses and autos, which burn fuel with oxygen inside them.
Kilns for firing clay pots, and furnaces for making steel and glass.
Crematoria and the burning of waste, which turn fuel into gases and ash.

open_questions.q: When did people first learn to make fire whenever they wanted, not just keep fires they found?
open_questions.why_open: Making fire leaves few traces, such as worn sticks or struck stones. Scientists are still looking for clear evidence.

open_questions.q: Did cooking help human brains grow larger?
open_questions.why_open: The idea fits some facts, but the oldest signs of fire do not go back as far as the first changes in our ancestors' bodies.

open_questions.q: What exactly happens, step by step, inside a flame?
open_questions.why_open: Even a candle flame involves hundreds of small chemical steps. Scientists use computers to model them, and some steps, such as exactly how soot forms, are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How will climate change alter wildfires?
open_questions.why_open: Hotter, drier weather makes fires more likely in many places, but how much depends on rain, plants and people, which are hard to predict.

maths.problem: In The Jumping Flame, Meenakshi's family tried each height 3 times. At 2 cm the flame jumped 3 times. At 5 cm it jumped 2 times. At 8 cm it jumped 1 time. How many jumps were there in all? What fraction of the tries at 5 cm worked?
maths.answer: 6 jumps in all. At 5 cm, 2 out of 3 tries worked, which is two thirds.
maths.explain: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 jumps. At 5 cm there were 3 tries, and 2 worked, so the fraction is 2 out of 3, or two thirds. The pattern shows the flame jumps less often the higher the match.
maths.context: This is about The Jumping Flame, where a match was held in candle smoke at different heights.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of tries that worked lets you compare the heights fairly, even if you tried some more often than others.

chart.title: Jumps out of 3 tries
chart.x: Height of the match above the wick

maths.problem: In Dry Wick or Oiled Wick?, the dry wick burned for 40 seconds. The oiled wick was still burning after 10 minutes. How many times as long did the oiled wick burn, at least?
maths.explain: 10 minutes is 10 times 60 seconds, which is 600 seconds. 600 divided by 40 is 15. The oiled wick was still burning, so it would have lasted even longer.
maths.context: This is about Dry Wick or Oiled Wick?, where you timed a dry wick and a wick in oil.
maths.why_maths: Changing both times into seconds and dividing shows just how much longer the oil made the wick last.

maths.problem: A tea light burns for about 4 hours. Lakshmi's family lights 6 tea lights at 6 in the evening on Karthigai Deepam. At what time will they go out? If they light one new tea light every 4 hours, how many do they need to keep one burning for a whole day of 24 hours?
maths.answer: About 10 at night. They need 6 tea lights for 24 hours.
maths.explain: 6 in the evening plus 4 hours is 10 at night. All 6 burn at the same time, so they all go out at about 10. For one light all day: 24 divided by 4 is 6 tea lights, one after the other.
maths.context: This is about how long a tea light's wax lasts as fuel.
maths.why_maths: Adding hours to a start time tells you when the fuel will run out, which is useful for planning a festival.

maths.problem: Anand's family practised their fire plan three times. It took them 90 seconds the first time, 70 seconds the second time and 50 seconds the third time. If the pattern goes on, how long might the fourth practice take? Why might it stop getting faster?
maths.answer: About 30 seconds, but it will stop getting faster at some point.
maths.explain: Each practice was 20 seconds faster: 90, 70, 50, so the next would be 30. But walking down the stairs always takes some time. So the times would level off instead of reaching zero.
maths.context: This is about the Family Fire Plan project, where you practise getting out of your home.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern lets you predict the next number, and thinking about the real world shows when a pattern must stop.

roots.context: We have tested what a candle really burns, and found what every fire needs. Now we ask what a flame tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A match held to a lump of wax only melted it. Yet a flame above a blown-out wick ran down the smoke and relit it. What burns is wax that heat has turned into a gas. A flame keeps going because its own heat makes more gas to burn.
deep_truth.habit: We think of fire as eating the solid wax, wood or oil, the way we eat a dosa. But a flame never burns a solid directly. It keeps making its own fuel, by heating the solid into gas.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Jumping Flame, a match held to a lump of wax for ten seconds only melted it. The same match lit the white smoke of a blown-out candle from a few centimetres above, and the flame ran down to the wick.

three.who_am_i: You belong to the only kind of animal that makes fire. For hundreds of thousands of years, people have cooked, kept warm and talked around a fire.
three.what_is_life: Some plants in Australia and South Africa grow where bushfires come often. After a fire the ground is open and sunny, so their seeds wait to sprout until they sense the smoke.
three.what_is_this_world: Fire needs oxygen, and nearly all the oxygen in the air was made by plants and tiny sea beings. Before there was enough of it, nothing on Earth could burn.

roots.thread: Wax, oil, wood and cooking gas look nothing alike. One is a solid, one a liquid, one a gas. Yet in a flame they all do the same thing. Heat turns each into gas, and each gas joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light. So one kind of change shows up as a diya's yellow leaf of light, the blue ring on a stove and a forest fire on a hill.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker of about 500 BCE, fragment 30 (Diels-Kranz numbering)
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus said the world is like an ever-living fire, kindled in measures and going out in measures.
teachings.link: A candle flame keeps the same shape for hours, yet the wax gas in it is new every moment. Heraclitus chose fire as his picture of something that stays itself only by always changing.

teachings.source: The Buddha's Fire Sermon, Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28
teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that the senses and the mind are on fire, burning with wanting. The word nirvana means the blowing out, or going out, of a fire.
teachings.link: A fire goes out when its fuel stops coming, as the dry wick did. The Buddha used this picture: when wanting stops feeding the fire, it goes out by itself.

science.text: Burning is fuel joining with oxygen. It gives out heat and light and makes carbon dioxide and water.
Charcoal in rocks shows wildfires on Earth over 400 million years ago, soon after plants spread onto land and raised the oxygen in the air.
When people first learned to make fire, and not just keep it, is still not known.

other_view.view: A flame is a chemical reaction that gives out enough heat to keep going. Calling it a flame that feeds itself, or comparing it with the world, adds nothing to the chemistry. It is wax gas and oxygen, and nothing more.

practice.title: Watching one flame
practice.say: A grown-up lights one candle on a steel plate. Let's sit an arm's length away. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Now just watch the flame for one minute. Notice its shape, its colours, the blue at the bottom. Every moment, new wax gas is flowing into it. Yet it looks the same. Breathe out gently, not at the flame. Now close your eyes. Can you still see it?

ask: The flame you see now is made of different gas from a minute ago. Is it the same flame?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Choices made: all lighting is done by a grown-up, on a steel plate on a bare counter, with a bowl of water nearby. The Jumping Flame uses plain white wax candles, which give the thickest smoke. The match is lit before the candle is blown out, because the smoke lasts only a second or two, and the fan must be off. The 2 cm height nearly always works, 5 cm often and 8 cm only sometimes, so the step says 'did not jump' is a result too. The wax lump may flicker for a moment from the match's own flame, so the step says to watch what happens when the match is taken away. The tea strainer must be all steel, as plastic rims melt, and is held for 3 seconds only. A slotted spoon with holes about half a centimetre wide lets flame tongues through. Kerosene and petrol are never used. The cup-over-the-candle test and the cold spoon test are left out, because they are in the edge-of-life unit. The water-on-oil danger is explained, never shown. The spine is the flame-watching activity, The Jumping Flame, the explanation cards, the home safety walk, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1800s, coal mines in England were full of danger. A gas called firedamp seeps out of coal, and a miner's candle could set it off. On 25 May 1812, an explosion at Felling Colliery, near Newcastle, killed 92 men and boys. Miners had tried other lights. A steel mill was a steel wheel spun against a flint, which threw out sparks to see by. It was thought to be safer than a candle, but explosions showed that sparks could light firedamp too. In 1815, the chemist Humphry Davy, helped by young Michael Faraday, studied how flames travel. He found that a flame could not pass through narrow metal tubes or fine wire mesh, because the metal took away its heat. So he put a lamp's flame inside a cylinder of iron mesh. The engineer George Stephenson made a similar lamp at the same time. Many then believed Davy's lamp made mines safe. But in 1835, a committee of the British Parliament found that accidents had gone up. Owners sent men into gassier parts of mines, and a draught or a broken wire could let the flame out.
how_we_found_out.who: Humphry Davy, a chemist in London, helped by Michael Faraday, and George Stephenson, a mine engineer in Killingworth
how_we_found_out.when: 1812 (the Felling Colliery explosion), 1815 to 1816 (the safety lamps), 1835 (the committee's report)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Miners first believed the sparks of a steel mill were a safe light in firedamp, but the explosion at Wallsend Colliery in 1785 showed that sparks could set it off. Later, many believed the Davy lamp made mines completely safe. The 1835 committee showed accidents had gone up, because a draught or a broken wire could let the flame out, and men were sent into more dangerous parts of the mines.
